blocks.title: This is the traditional way
blocks.text: This guide shows how traditional farmers usually plant suha. Use it as a starting point. For a higher yield, update it: plant certified seed or clean planting material, test your soil, and follow the right spacing and fertilizer.

This guide shows how Filipino growers usually plant pomelo from a marcot or grafted seedling and care for it until it bears fruit worth selling. It is for backyards and small orchards, such as the Magallanes pomelo farms of Davao.

Before you plant, get the field ready with our [land preparation guide for fruit and plantation trees](/land-preparation/fruit-tree-land-preparation). Then choose your seed or planting material with the [suha varieties sold here](/crop-varieties/pomelo). If the leaves turn pale later on, the [suha nutrient deficiency guide](/nutrient-deficiencies/pomelo-nutrient-deficiency) helps you find what is missing. For more on the crop, read [pagtatanim ng puno](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-puno).
When to plant suha

Marcots and seedlings are planted as the rains begin, around May to July, so they root before the dry months. In Davao and other places where rain spreads through the year, planting goes on in most wet months.
What you plant

Most growers plant a marcot (air layer) taken from a heavy bearing tree with sweet, juicy fruit, or a grafted seedling on a hardy rootstock. Some growers prefer big marcots, over 1.5 m tall, because they survive well and may give a few fruits within a year. Trees grown from seed take long to bear and the fruit can differ from the mother tree.
Paano magtanim ng suha, step by step
A pomelo tree gives enough fruit to sell at about 4 years from planting. Big marcots may give a few fruits in the first year or two. The crop is ready about 4 years after planting.
Before planting (Bago magtanim)

items.title: 2 months before planting: Clear the land and mark the spots
items.text: Clear the land and mark the planting spots about 8 to 10 m apart, since pomelo grows into a big tree. Pick ground that drains well. On slopes follow the contour.

items.title: 30 days before planting: Dig and fill the holes
items.text: Dig each hole about 50 cm wide and 50 cm deep and keep the topsoil apart. Mix the topsoil with compost or dried manure and put it back to settle before planting.

items.title: 7 days before planting: Pick and harden the marcot
items.text: Choose a marcot or grafted seedling with plenty of roots, healthy dark leaves and no gum on the bark. Keep it in light shade and water it daily for some days so it gets used to the field.

blocks.text: The nursery (Punlaan)

items.title: 5 months before planting: Make your own marcots (pagmamarcot)
items.text: Growers who have a sweet, juicy, heavy bearing tree often root their own marcots on it in the rainy months. Some prefer big marcots, since they survive well in the field.

parts.title: Choose the mother tree and the branch
parts.text: Pick a tree that bears every year, with good fruit and no pests or disease, and not too old. On it choose a branch about as thick as a finger or a little more, neither too young nor too old, growing upward in the sun, with no flowers or fruit on it.

parts.title: Mix the rooting ball
parts.text: Mix garden soil with rice hull, or with mudpress from a sugar mill or coir dust where you can get it. Wet it until it holds together when squeezed but does not drip.

parts.title: Peel a ring of bark
parts.text: With a clean, sharp knife, cut twice around the branch a short distance apart and peel off the bark between the cuts. Scrape off the slippery green layer under the bark too, or the bark heals over instead of making roots.

parts.title: Wrap and tie
parts.text: Hold a piece of clear plastic around the branch below the ring, pack a ball of the moist mix over the whole ring, close the plastic around it and tie both ends tightly with plastic straw.

parts.title: Wait for the roots
parts.text: Leave the wrap on the tree and look at it every week or two. The marcot is ready when white roots show plainly all around the ball through the plastic. If the ball dries, open the top and add a little water.

parts.title: Cut it and bag it
parts.text: Cut the branch just below the ball with sharp shears or a saw. Take off the plastic gently, without breaking the ball, and plant it in a 6 by 8 inch bag of two parts soil, one part compost and one part rice hull.

parts.title: Nurse it in the shade
parts.text: Keep the new plant in the shade, out of the rain, and water it daily. After two weeks move it where it gets some sun, and pick off any flowers so it grows roots and leaves first. Tip: A big marcot needs a bigger bag or pot than the 6 by 8 inch size, so its roots are not cramped.

blocks.text: Planting day (Pagtatanim)

items.title: Planting day: Plant and stake
items.text: Remove the bag or wrapping without breaking the soil ball and set the plant at the depth it grew. Firm the soil, water well and tie the plant to a strong stake against the wind.

blocks.text: Care while it grows (Pag aalaga)

items.title: Day 3: Shade, mulch and water
items.text: Shade the new tree with fronds for a few weeks and mulch around it, a little away from the stem. Water every few days in dry weather until new leaves show.

items.title: Day 30: First feeding
items.text: About a month after planting, spread a small amount of complete fertilizer or ammonium sulfate around the tree and mix it lightly into the soil. Feed again every three to four months, a little more each year, with manure when you have it.

items.title: Day 45: Weed around the young tree
items.text: Keep a clean circle around the tree by hand or bolo. Short crops can be grown between the young trees.

items.title: Month 3: Check new leaves and bark
items.text: Look at each new flush for aphids, psyllids and leaf miners, and at the trunk for gum oozing from the bark. Cut and burn badly hit twigs and keep the base dry and clean.

items.title: Month 9: Shape the young tree
items.text: Cut back the tips to make the tree branch, keep a few strong main branches and remove water sprouts and branches that touch the ground. Pick off early fruits so the tree builds its frame first.

items.title: Month 12: Feed more as the tree grows
items.text: From the second year, feed the tree at the start and the end of the rains, spreading the fertilizer under the outer leaves. Bearing trees need more potash for sweet, juicy fruit.

blocks.text: Harvest (Anihan)

items.title: Year 4: First good harvest
items.text: Pick when the fruit is full sized, the skin turns lighter green or yellowish and the oil glands look smooth and shiny. Cut the stem with a pruning knife or a pole cutter so the fruit does not drop.

blocks.text: Spacing, water and fertilizer for suha
Spacing
About 8 to 10 m between trees, often 10 m by 10 m, or 8 to 10 m between rows and 6 to 8 m in the row. Holes about 50 cm wide and deep, one plant a hole.
Water
Mostly rain fed. New trees are watered every few days in dry weather and mulched. Growers who can water during flowering and fruit growth in dry spells get better fruit set.
Fertilizer

Compost or dried manure in the hole at planting. Young trees get a little complete fertilizer or ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) every three to four months, more each year. Bearing trees get fertilizer with more potash, plus micronutrients, at the start and end of the rains. Growers note that the wrong feeding gives thick rind and dry, bland flesh. To read what a bag really gives, see our guide to [fertilizer for this crop](/blog/fertilizer-for-fruit-trees).
Care and harvest
Care while it grows

Staking, mulching and weeding around young trees, light pruning to remove water sprouts, dead twigs and branches that touch the ground, and heavier pruning right after the main harvest. Thinning fruits that come in clusters so the rest grow big. Checking new flushes for aphids and psyllids and the trunk for gum. Many growers bag the young fruits against fruit flies and rind borers.
When and how to harvest

Pomelo needs no flower inducer and can give a main crop and a smaller off season crop each year. Fruit is picked when full sized, with lighter colored, smooth, shiny skin, by cutting the stem rather than pulling. The fruit keeps a month or more in a cool, shaded place, and is handled gently so the rind does not bruise.
Common mistakes when planting suha

items: Planting seedlings from seed, which bear late and give fruits unlike the mother tree.
Taking marcots from a sour or poor bearing tree.
Planting too close, so the big trees shade each other.
Letting every fruit in a cluster grow, so all stay small.
Giving the wrong fertilizer, which gives thick rind and dry flesh.
Leaving fruit flies and rind borers unchecked in the orchard.

blocks.text: How to get a higher yield of suha
The traditional way gets a crop, but small changes add up. These are the first things to change, one season at a time.

items: Buy marcots or grafted seedlings from an accredited nursery or a proven mother tree.
Test the soil and feed by the result, with enough potash and micronutrients.
Prune right after the main harvest and thin fruit clusters.
Bag young fruits and keep fallen fruit cleaned up against fruit flies and rind borers.
Water during flowering and fruit growth in long dry spells.
Scout every new flush for aphids and psyllids that spread citrus diseases.

items.q: When do farmers plant suha in the Philippines?
items.a: Marcots and seedlings are planted as the rains begin, around May to July, so they root before the dry months. In Davao and other places where rain spreads through the year, planting goes on in most wet months.

items.a: About 8 to 10 m between trees, often 10 m by 10 m, or 8 to 10 m between rows and 6 to 8 m in the row. Holes about 50 cm wide and deep, one plant a hole.

items.q: How long before suha can be harvested?
items.a: It is ready about 4 years after planting. Pomelo needs no flower inducer and can give a main crop and a smaller off season crop each year.
